evidence:
PLAN (partial): the H0 does name it — 'positive channel checks carry no information beyond what is already in point-in-time consensus and price' — and Step 3 'what is already priced' does the revision/price work: 'if three or more analysts have already raised FY numbers above the company guide, the sell-side has pre-baked the raise and the surprise is gone' and 'the channel-check information has already been disseminated and monetized.' But it is Step 3 of 5, subordinate to a Step 1 arithmetic gate, and the plan still scopes a full week: a 16-20 quarter point-in-time ledger, a '1,500-2,500 firm-quarter' panel, '150-250 hand-coded episodes; that is one analyst-week', a Firth-penalized logit, Fama-French five-factor event study, and five alternative-data corroboration pulls. It also frames the priced question as a crowding filter ('pre-print excess return versus the peer basket is under +4%') rather than as the distributional point that published research is consensus by construction. Credit where due: (b) is the plan's best hour — 'expansion within existing accounts is 70-90% of net new ARR... levered to 10-30% of the growth engine'; (c) is genuinely well done — 'Companies have persistent guidance philosophies. A CFO who has flowed through 0.6x for eight straight quarters is not going to flow through 1.4x because a VAR told a broker things feel good'; (d) is explicit — 'Distribution partners agree to talk when business is good and go quiet when it is not... The observed sample of positive checks is therefore not a random draw.'

CRITIQUE (caught): the consensus-by-construction point is stated flatly under 'Is the idea worth a full project?' — 'No. Not as stated... Layer on the fact that these are firm-approved third-party notes — every entitled fund has them — and the informational edge is close to zero by construction. The plan is correct that the only version with real edge is proprietary checks, and correct not to go there.' Guidance-as-policy is carried in the cheap version: 'The question it answers: has this CFO *ever* raised by more than the beat, and in which fiscal quarter?' and in problem 6, which identifies the policy trade-off the checks themselves imply — 'a genuine new-logo surge argues for a better revenue guide and a worse EPS guide simultaneously.' It also kills the escape hatch that would have let the analyst be involved anyway: 'As written it converts a disciplined plan into "we found a reason to be involved."'
missed: Never says the obvious non-answer out loud: a good quarter with no raise is the modal Q1/Q2 outcome and is not bearish. Both documents treat 'no incremental raise' as thesis failure; neither tells the PM that the stock routinely trades fine through it, or that the real short-side risk is an in-line print into a pre-baked raise, not the absence of a raise per se.

Does not push the priced question to position one. The critique keeps 'what's priced' as item 3 of 3 in the half-day, behind 90 minutes of ACV arithmetic. On a published-note seed the order is inverted: check the tape and the revision tape first, because if the print date is inside 30 days and numbers are already above the guide, the sizing arithmetic is moot and you never spend the 90 minutes.

Ignores the cheapest single datapoint on the desk: what the publishing brokers did with their own numbers and price targets when the checks went out. A check note that came with an estimate raise is the revision; one that did not is a broker with nothing to sell. Neither document reads the notes as artifacts with timestamps and attached estimate changes.

Leaves the sampling critique where the plan put it and adds nothing. A desk would press further: VAR/reseller checks sample the channel, which in most enterprise software is a minority of bookings versus direct sales, so the checks may be well-sourced about a slice that does not drive the guide. The critique accepts the plan's selection paragraph as adequate.

No treatment of the actual expression if the work concludes 'priced.' The interesting trade in a crowded-positive-checks setup is the fade or the vol structure, and the critique deletes the positioning override without replacing it with the one thing a PM would ask: what is the payoff to being short the setup?

Never asks the desk-hygiene questions that would resolve this in ten minutes: does the book already own it, what is the print date, is the name in a quiet period, and did the company pre-announce or present at a conference after the checks published.

Does not challenge whether the checks even map onto FY revenue timing. Enterprise logos ramp through implementation and go-live; the critique fixes the recognition-lag arithmetic but never asks the analyst to get the actual ramp schedule or PS-attach from the last two cohorts, which is the only version of (b) that is checkable rather than assumed.
manufactured: Problem 7's probability arithmetic is wrong as written: 'With five noisy roughly-binary proxies, the chance that at least three point the same direction under the null is around a coin flip.' At least three of five agreeing in direction happens with probability 1 by pigeonhole; the ~50% figure is P(at least 3 positive). The underlying complaint — that a 3-of-5 vote is a gate that always passes — is real and worth keeping, but the number attached to it is not.

Problem 4 overstates: the scalable proxy is called 'identical to the crowding control in Step 3.' Step 3's crowding measure is 20-day excess return, short interest, borrow and implied move, with revision trajectory as one component. Correlated, not identical; the within-strata fix it proposes is sound regardless.
verdict_line: Plan builds a month of machinery to price a published broker note; critique correctly cuts it to half a day and says the edge is zero by construction — but both bury the only question that matters (what have estimates and the tape already done since the checks hit) behind arithmetic nobody will need.
